Allan Variance: The Time-Domain Counterpart of Phase Noise

Prerequisites: psd_phase_noise_jitter · white_noise_to_phase_noise ｜ Next: serdes_clocking_connection

The previous pages all viewed oscillator imperfection from the frequency domain: jitter was written as SSB phase noise L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf) (in dBc/Hz) or as the phase PSD Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) (in rad2/Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}rad2/Hz), then integrated into an rms jitter σt\sigma_tσt​ (see psd_phase_noise_jitter). That language is the natural one for RF/communication circuits. But the people who work on clocks, frequency standards, GPS, and atomic clocks speak another language: the Allan variance and its square root, the Allan deviation / ADEV σy(τ)\sigma_y(\tau)σy​(τ). This page answers:

  • What does σy(τ)\sigma_y(\tau)σy​(τ) actually measure? Why is it defined as the mean square of the "difference between two adjacent gated frequency averages"?
  • How does it convert to the familiar Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) and L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf)?
  • Why does each of the five power-law noise types trace a characteristic slope on the ADEV log–log plot, so that the slopes "read out the noise type at a glance"?
  • Why does the clock community prefer ADEV over the ordinary sample variance of frequency?

Physical intuition (conclusion first): take a stopwatch (the oscillator under test) and compare it against a perfect clock; every τ\tauτ seconds record "over this τ\tauτ-second gate, how much faster/slower was my average frequency than nominal", producing a string of fractional frequency deviations yˉk\bar y_kyˉ​k​. The ordinary variance asks "how far are these yˉk\bar y_kyˉ​k​ from their grand mean" — but for flicker (1/f1/f1/f) and random-walk noise, the grand mean simply does not exist (it keeps drifting the longer you collect data), so the ordinary variance grows and grows without converging. Allan's trick: do not compare against the grand mean — compare only against the neighboring gate — 12⟨(yˉk+1−yˉk)2⟩\tfrac12\langle(\bar y_{k+1}-\bar y_k)^2\rangle21​⟨(yˉ​k+1​−yˉ​k​)2⟩. The adjacent subtraction cancels out the "slow drift", so even for flicker/RW noise the result converges and can be measured repeatably as a stable number. The price: it becomes a function of τ\tauτ — the gate length τ\tauτ you choose sets the time scale at which you probe stability.

ADEV is "phase noise in the time domain": the same physics (the same Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f)), just viewed in a different coordinate. Below we connect the two sides step by step.

Step 1: the fractional frequency deviation y(t)y(t)y(t) and its PSD Sy(f)S_y(f)Sy​(f)​

First, define the protagonist. Let the instantaneous phase of the signal under test be ω0t+ϕ(t)\omega_0 t+\phi(t)ω0​t+ϕ(t), where ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) is the excess phase (the random offset relative to the ideal linear phase, in rad). The instantaneous fractional frequency deviation (dimensionless) is defined as the time derivative of the phase deviation divided by the nominal angular frequency:

y(t)=1ω0dϕ(t)dt=12πf0 ϕ˙(t).y(t)=\frac{1}{\omega_0}\frac{d\phi(t)}{dt}=\frac{1}{2\pi f_0}\,\dot\phi(t).y(t)=ω0​1​dtdϕ(t)​=2πf0​1​ϕ˙​(t).
  • Physical meaning: yyy is "by what fraction the frequency right now exceeds the nominal frequency". y=10−9y=10^{-9}y=10−9 means the frequency is off by 1 ppb (one part per billion).
  • Unit check: ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​ is rad/s\text{rad/s}rad/s, ω0\omega_0ω0​ is rad/s\text{rad/s}rad/s; the ratio is dimensionless ✓. yyy being dimensionless is exactly what "fractional" means.

Relation between the PSD of yyy and the PSD of ϕ\phiϕ. Differentiation multiplies by j2πfj2\pi fj2πf in the frequency domain, so the power spectrum is multiplied by the squared magnitude (2πf)2(2\pi f)^2(2πf)2. Hence (spec §11.2):

Sy(f)=(2πf)2(2πf0)2 Sϕ(f)=f2f02 Sϕ(f).S_y(f)=\frac{(2\pi f)^2}{(2\pi f_0)^2}\,S_\phi(f)=\frac{f^2}{f_0^2}\,S_\phi(f).Sy​(f)=(2πf0​)2(2πf)2​Sϕ​(f)=f02​f2​Sϕ​(f).
  • Math used: for a stationary process a(t)→a˙(t)a(t)\to\dot a(t)a(t)→a˙(t), the PSD is multiplied by ∣j2πf∣2=(2πf)2|j2\pi f|^2=(2\pi f)^2∣j2πf∣2=(2πf)2 (the LTI filter H(f)=j2πfH(f)=j2\pi fH(f)=j2πf).
  • Unit check: SϕS_\phiSϕ​ is rad2/Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}rad2/Hz; multiplied by the dimensionless f2/f02f^2/f_0^2f2/f02​, SyS_ySy​ has units 1/Hz1/\text{Hz}1/Hz (the PSD of a dimensionless quantity) ✓.
  • Key marker: this Sy=(f2/f02)SϕS_y=(f^2/f_0^2)S_\phiSy​=(f2/f02​)Sϕ​ is the adapter between "phase noise ↔ frequency noise" — the entire slope table below hinges on it. Differentiation adds 2 to the power of fff: Sϕ∼f−2S_\phi\sim f^{-2}Sϕ​∼f−2 (our signature 1/f21/f^21/f2) corresponds to Sy∼f0S_y\sim f^{0}Sy​∼f0 (white FM).

Step 2: definition of the two-sample (Allan) variance​

Slice the continuous y(t)y(t)y(t) into gates of length τ\tauτ; the average fractional frequency of the kkk-th gate is

yˉk=1τ∫tktk+τy(t) dt=x(tk+τ)−x(tk)τ,x(t)≡∫ty(t′) dt′=ϕ(t)2πf0.\bar y_k=\frac{1}{\tau}\int_{t_k}^{t_k+\tau}y(t)\,dt=\frac{x(t_k+\tau)-x(t_k)}{\tau}, \qquad x(t)\equiv\int^{t}y(t')\,dt'=\frac{\phi(t)}{2\pi f_0}.yˉ​k​=τ1​∫tk​tk​+τ​y(t)dt=τx(tk​+τ)−x(tk​)​,x(t)≡∫ty(t′)dt′=2πf0​ϕ(t)​.

Here x(t)x(t)x(t) is the time error (the accumulated time offset of the clock under test relative to an ideal clock, in s) — note that it is exactly the phase divided by 2πf02\pi f_02πf0​, i.e. the Δt=Δϕ/(2πf0)\Delta t=\Delta\phi/(2\pi f_0)Δt=Δϕ/(2πf0​) of psd_phase_noise_jitter. So yˉk\bar y_kyˉ​k​ is nothing but "the difference of the time error at two adjacent instants, divided by the gate length".

The two-sample (Allan) variance is defined as the mean square of the difference between adjacent gated frequency averages, times 12\tfrac1221​ (spec §11.2):

σy2(τ)=⟨12(yˉk+1−yˉk)2⟩.\sigma_y^2(\tau)=\Big\langle\tfrac12\big(\bar y_{k+1}-\bar y_k\big)^2\Big\rangle.σy2​(τ)=⟨21​(yˉ​k+1​−yˉ​k​)2⟩.

ADEV is its square root, σy(τ)=σy2(τ)\sigma_y(\tau)=\sqrt{\sigma_y^2(\tau)}σy​(τ)=σy2​(τ)​.

  • What the 12\tfrac1221​ is for: if yˉk+1\bar y_{k+1}yˉ​k+1​ and yˉk\bar y_kyˉ​k​ are mutually independent, each with variance σ2\sigma^2σ2, then ⟨(yˉk+1−yˉk)2⟩=2σ2\langle(\bar y_{k+1}-\bar y_k)^2\rangle=2\sigma^2⟨(yˉ​k+1​−yˉ​k​)2⟩=2σ2, and the factor 12\tfrac1221​ restores exactly σ2\sigma^2σ2. In other words, for white FM (independent adjacent gates) this normalization makes ADEV equal to the classical standard deviation — Allan chose it deliberately so that in the most common case the two languages agree numerically.
  • Why "adjacent differences": differencing is a high-pass operation that blocks DC and very low frequencies (slow drift, aging, the unknown grand mean). This is the secret of its convergence even for flicker/RW noise (detailed in Step 5).
  • Unit check: yˉ\bar yyˉ​ dimensionless → σy2\sigma_y^2σy2​ dimensionless, σy\sigma_yσy​ dimensionless ✓.

Written as a "second difference" of the time error xxx. Substituting yˉk=[x(tk+τ)−x(tk)]/τ\bar y_k=[x(t_{k}+\tau)-x(t_k)]/\tauyˉ​k​=[x(tk​+τ)−x(tk​)]/τ, for adjacent gates (tk+1=tk+τt_{k+1}=t_k+\tautk+1​=tk​+τ):

yˉk+1−yˉk=xk+2−2xk+1+xkτ,\bar y_{k+1}-\bar y_k=\frac{x_{k+2}-2x_{k+1}+x_k}{\tau},yˉ​k+1​−yˉ​k​=τxk+2​−2xk+1​+xk​​,

where xk≡x(tk)x_k\equiv x(t_k)xk​≡x(tk​) and the sampling interval is τ\tauτ. The numerator xk+2−2xk+1+xkx_{k+2}-2x_{k+1}+x_kxk+2​−2xk+1​+xk​ is exactly the second difference of the time error (a discrete second derivative). This is precisely what the line d = x[2m:] - 2*x[m:-m] + x[:-2m] does in the simulation script lab_19_allan.py.

Step 3: moving the definition to the frequency domain — the transfer-function kernel sin⁡4(πfτ)/(πfτ)2\sin^4(\pi f\tau)/(\pi f\tau)^2sin4(πfτ)/(πfτ)2​

The target we want to prove is (spec §11.2):

σy2(τ)=2∫0∞Sy(f) sin⁡4(πfτ)(πfτ)2 df.\sigma_y^2(\tau)=2\int_0^{\infty}S_y(f)\,\frac{\sin^4(\pi f\tau)}{(\pi f\tau)^2}\,df.σy2​(τ)=2∫0∞​Sy​(f)(πfτ)2sin4(πfτ)​df.

Derivation strategy: σy2(τ)\sigma_y^2(\tau)σy2​(τ) is the power of a linearly filtered signal, and the power after linear filtering =∫Sin(f) ∣H(f)∣2 df=\int S_{\text{in}}(f)\,|H(f)|^2\,df=∫Sin​(f)∣H(f)∣2df. We only need to find the transfer function H(f)H(f)H(f) of the operation "from y(t)y(t)y(t) to 12(yˉk+1−yˉk)\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\bar y_{k+1}-\bar y_k)2​1​(yˉ​k+1​−yˉ​k​)" and compute its ∣H(f)∣2|H(f)|^2∣H(f)∣2.

Step (i): gate averaging = convolution with a rectangular window. yˉk=1τ∫tktk+τy dt\bar y_k=\frac1\tau\int_{t_k}^{t_k+\tau}y\,dtyˉ​k​=τ1​∫tk​tk​+τ​ydt is yyy convolved with a rectangular window of width τ\tauτ and height 1/τ1/\tau1/τ, sampled at tkt_ktk​. The frequency response of the rectangular window is a sinc:

Havg(f)=1τ∫0τe−j2πft dt=e−jπfτ sin⁡(πfτ)πfτ.H_{\text{avg}}(f)=\frac{1}{\tau}\int_0^{\tau}e^{-j2\pi f t}\,dt=e^{-j\pi f\tau}\,\frac{\sin(\pi f\tau)}{\pi f\tau}.Havg​(f)=τ1​∫0τ​e−j2πftdt=e−jπfτπfτsin(πfτ)​.
  • Math used: rectangular window ↔\leftrightarrow↔ sinc (a basic Fourier-transform pair).
  • sin⁡(πfτ)πfτ\dfrac{\sin(\pi f\tau)}{\pi f\tau}πfτsin(πfτ)​ is the normalized sinc; the prefactor e−jπfτe^{-j\pi f\tau}e−jπfτ is the linear phase due to the window center.

Step (ii): adjacent subtraction = multiplication by a first-difference kernel. yˉk+1−yˉk\bar y_{k+1}-\bar y_kyˉ​k+1​−yˉ​k​ shifts the same gate average by τ\tauτ and subtracts, which in the frequency domain multiplies by (e−j2πfτ−1)\big(e^{-j2\pi f\tau}-1\big)(e−j2πfτ−1), whose squared magnitude is

∣e−j2πfτ−1∣2=2−2cos⁡(2πfτ)=4sin⁡2(πfτ).\big|e^{-j2\pi f\tau}-1\big|^2=2-2\cos(2\pi f\tau)=4\sin^2(\pi f\tau).​e−j2πfτ−1​2=2−2cos(2πfτ)=4sin2(πfτ).

(Using the half-angle identity 1−cos⁡2θ=2sin⁡2θ1-\cos2\theta=2\sin^2\theta1−cos2θ=2sin2θ with θ=πfτ\theta=\pi f\tauθ=πfτ.)

Step (iii): multiply the three pieces together. The overall operation g(t)=12(yˉk+1−yˉk)g(t)=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\bar y_{k+1}-\bar y_k)g(t)=2​1​(yˉ​k+1​−yˉ​k​) (the 12\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}2​1​ is the square root of the 12\tfrac1221​ in the definition) has the transfer-function magnitude squared:

∣H(f)∣2=12⏟def. 12⋅(sin⁡(πfτ)πfτ)2⏟gate average⋅4sin⁡2(πfτ)⏟adjacent difference=2sin⁡4(πfτ)(πfτ)2.|H(f)|^2=\underbrace{\tfrac12}_{\text{def.}\,\frac12}\cdot\underbrace{\Big(\frac{\sin(\pi f\tau)}{\pi f\tau}\Big)^2}_{\text{gate average}}\cdot\underbrace{4\sin^2(\pi f\tau)}_{\text{adjacent difference}}=\frac{2\sin^4(\pi f\tau)}{(\pi f\tau)^2}.∣H(f)∣2=def.21​21​​​⋅gate average(πfτsin(πfτ)​)2​​⋅adjacent difference4sin2(πfτ)​​=(πfτ)22sin4(πfτ)​.

Step (iv): apply Wiener–Khinchin (power = ∫ PSD × |H|²). Using the single-sided PSD (∫0∞\int_0^\infty∫0∞​):

σy2(τ)=∫0∞Sy(f) ∣H(f)∣2 df=2∫0∞Sy(f) sin⁡4(πfτ)(πfτ)2 df.✓\sigma_y^2(\tau)=\int_0^{\infty}S_y(f)\,|H(f)|^2\,df=2\int_0^{\infty}S_y(f)\,\frac{\sin^4(\pi f\tau)}{(\pi f\tau)^2}\,df.\qquad\checkmarkσy2​(τ)=∫0∞​Sy​(f)∣H(f)∣2df=2∫0∞​Sy​(f)(πfτ)2sin4(πfτ)​df.✓

This is the frequency-domain integral of spec §11.2.

  • Physical meaning: sin⁡4/(⋅)2\sin^4/(\cdot)^2sin4/(⋅)2 is a band-pass kernel: near f→0f\to0f→0 it behaves like f2f^2f2 (high-pass, blocking slow drift), at high frequency like 1/f21/f^21/f2 (low-pass, suppressing ultra-fast noise), with its peak near fτ∼0.5f\tau\sim 0.5fτ∼0.5. Choosing τ\tauτ means choosing which frequency band this band-pass looks at — large τ\tauτ probes low frequencies, small τ\tauτ high frequencies.
  • Unit check: SyS_ySy​ is 1/Hz1/\text{Hz}1/Hz, the kernel is dimensionless, dfdfdf is Hz; the integral is dimensionless → σy2\sigma_y^2σy2​ dimensionless ✓.

This is the bridge showing "time domain ↔ frequency domain are the same thing": given any Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f), first convert it to SyS_ySy​ via Step 1, then substitute into this integral to get ADEV; conversely, a measured ADEV can be inverted back to SyS_ySy​ and SϕS_\phiSϕ​. The entire slope table below is nothing but this integral evaluated for power laws Sy∼fαS_y\sim f^\alphaSy​∼fα.

Step 4: the ADEV slope table for the five power-law noise types​

The frequency-standards community writes noise as a superposition of power laws (the power-law model). Each type is described by Sy(f)=hαfαS_y(f)=h_\alpha f^\alphaSy​(f)=hα​fα, with α\alphaα running from −2-2−2 to +2+2+2. Substituting each into the Step-3 integral gives the characteristic slope σy(τ)∝τμ\sigma_y(\tau)\propto\tau^\muσy​(τ)∝τμ. The table below is the core reference table of frequency metrology (PM = phase modulation, FM = frequency modulation):

Noise typeSϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) slopeSy(f)=f2f02SϕS_y(f)=\frac{f^2}{f_0^2}S_\phiSy​(f)=f02​f2​Sϕ​ slopeσy2(τ)∝\sigma_y^2(\tau)\proptoσy2​(τ)∝ADEV σy(τ)∝\sigma_y(\tau)\proptoσy​(τ)∝
white PMf0f^{0}f0f+2f^{+2}f+2τ−2\tau^{-2}τ−2τ−1\tau^{-1}τ−1
flicker PMf−1f^{-1}f−1f+1f^{+1}f+1τ−2\tau^{-2}τ−2 (with ln⁡\lnln correction)τ−1\tau^{-1}τ−1
white FMf−2f^{-2}f−2f0f^{0}f0τ−1\tau^{-1}τ−1τ−1/2\tau^{-1/2}τ−1/2
flicker FMf−3f^{-3}f−3f−1f^{-1}f−1τ0\tau^{0}τ0τ0\tau^{0}τ0 (floor)
random-walk FMf−4f^{-4}f−4f−2f^{-2}f−2τ+1\tau^{+1}τ+1τ+1/2\tau^{+1/2}τ+1/2

Note the single most important row: our signature white FM (Sϕ∼1/f2S_\phi\sim1/f^2Sϕ​∼1/f2, produced from white noise by phase integration; see white_noise_to_phase_noise) corresponds to an ADEV slope of τ−1/2\tau^{-1/2}τ−1/2. In other words, the −20-20−20 dB/decade phase-noise skirt appears on the time-domain ADEV plot as a line of slope −1/2-1/2−1/2.

Why each slope is what it is​

(a) white FM → τ−1/2\tau^{-1/2}τ−1/2 (the one to remember). Sy∼f0S_y\sim f^0Sy​∼f0 is white; y(t)y(t)y(t) is white noise. yˉk\bar y_kyˉ​k​ averages white noise over a gate τ\tauτ — averaging NNN independent samples of white noise reduces the variance by 1/N∝1/τ1/N\propto1/\tau1/N∝1/τ, hence σy2∝1/τ\sigma_y^2\propto1/\tauσy2​∝1/τ and σy∝τ−1/2\sigma_y\propto\tau^{-1/2}σy​∝τ−1/2. Intuition: the longer you measure, the steadier the average — the standard error falls like 1/τ1/\sqrt{\tau}1/τ​; this is the familiar N\sqrt NN​ law of "under white frequency noise, longer averaging is more accurate". Equivalently, yyy white ⇒ the time error x=∫yx=\int yx=∫y is a random walk; the variance of adjacent-gate differences ∝τ\propto\tau∝τ, and dividing by τ2\tau^2τ2 gives ∝1/τ\propto1/\tau∝1/τ.

(b) flicker FM → τ0\tau^{0}τ0 (the floor). Sy∼1/fS_y\sim1/fSy​∼1/f (1/f1/f1/f frequency noise). The remarkable property of a 1/f1/f1/f process is scale invariance: it looks statistically the same at every time scale. Feed it into the band-pass kernel and the integral comes out independent of τ\tauτ — ADEV becomes a horizontal line. Intuition: the device's 1/f1/f1/f (flicker) noise upconverts into 1/f31/f^31/f3 phase noise (see flicker_noise_upconversion); in the time domain it becomes the floor where "no amount of extra averaging time makes you any more stable". This floor is the fundamental limit of long-term stability in quartz/atomic oscillators, known in engineering as the flicker floor.

(c) random-walk FM → τ+1/2\tau^{+1/2}τ+1/2 (heading upward). Sy∼1/f2S_y\sim1/f^2Sy​∼1/f2; y(t)y(t)y(t) itself is a random walk (integrated white noise). The longer the averaging time, the further yyy itself has already wandered, so the adjacent-gate differences actually grow: σy2∝τ\sigma_y^2\propto\tauσy2​∝τ, σy∝τ+1/2\sigma_y\propto\tau^{+1/2}σy​∝τ+1/2. Intuition: temperature drift, precursors of aging — low-frequency processes that "wander ever farther" — get worse the longer you measure. The right half of an ADEV plot bending upward is usually this.

(d) white PM and flicker PM → both τ−1\tau^{-1}τ−1 (steepest, left side). PM-type noise is concentrated at high frequency (Sy∼f+2S_y\sim f^{+2}Sy​∼f+2, f+1f^{+1}f+1) and is strongly suppressed by the sinc2\text{sinc}^2sinc2 of the gate average, so it drops off quickly as τ\tauτ is stretched: ADEV ∝τ−1\propto\tau^{-1}∝τ−1 (steeper than white FM's τ−1/2\tau^{-1/2}τ−1/2). Intuition: pure phase noise (e.g., additive white noise of the measurement system, buffer thermal noise) is prominent at small τ\tauτ and gets averaged away at large τ\tauτ. Note: white PM and flicker PM have the same ADEV slope (both τ−1\tau^{-1}τ−1) and cannot be distinguished — this is a real weakness of ADEV, which motivated the improved MDEV (modified Allan deviation): under MDEV, white PM follows τ−3/2\tau^{-3/2}τ−3/2 and flicker PM follows τ−1\tau^{-1}τ−1, making them separable (MDEV is an extension topic not developed here).

Mnemonic: from left to right, as τ\tauτ grows from small to large, the ADEV slope walks −1→−1/2→0→+1/2-1\to-1/2\to0\to+1/2−1→−1/2→0→+1/2 — a bathtub curve that "drops, bottoms out, then climbs". The minimum at the bottom corresponds to the optimal averaging time τopt\tau_{\text{opt}}τopt​ — the τ\tauτ to pick for the most stable measurement or timekeeping.

Step 5: why does the clock community use ADEV instead of the ordinary frequency variance?​

This is the "why" at the heart of this page. Suppose you want the most intuitive description of frequency stability: take MMM frequency samples yˉk\bar y_kyˉ​k​ and compute the ordinary sample variance (also called the N-sample / standard variance)

σstd2(M,τ)=1M−1∑k=1M(yˉk−yˉ‾)2,yˉ‾=1M∑kyˉk.\sigma^2_{\text{std}}(M,\tau)=\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_{k=1}^{M}\big(\bar y_k-\overline{\bar y}\big)^2,\qquad\overline{\bar y}=\frac1M\sum_k\bar y_k.σstd2​(M,τ)=M−11​k=1∑M​(yˉ​k​−yˉ​​)2,yˉ​​=M1​k∑​yˉ​k​.

The problem is that it subtracts the "grand mean" yˉ‾\overline{\bar y}yˉ​​.

For white FM, no problem. White FM is stationary, yˉ‾\overline{\bar y}yˉ​​ converges to the true value, and σstd2\sigma^2_{\text{std}}σstd2​ converges too, consistent with ADEV.

For flicker FM and random-walk FM it blows up. These two have strong (even divergent) low-frequency energy:

  • They are non-ergodic in the mean: yˉ‾\overline{\bar y}yˉ​​ does not converge; the longer you measure and the larger MMM gets, the more yˉ‾\overline{\bar y}yˉ​​ itself keeps drifting.
  • Consequently σstd2(M,τ)\sigma^2_{\text{std}}(M,\tau)σstd2​(M,τ) grows monotonically with the sample count MMM and never converges — the "frequency instability" you report depends on "how long you measured", which is a metrological disaster (not repeatable, not comparable).
  • Mathematically: the equivalent kernel of the standard variance against Sy(f)S_y(f)Sy​(f) behaves only like f0f^0f0 as f→0f\to0f→0 (DC is not blocked); against Sy∼1/fS_y\sim1/fSy​∼1/f or 1/f21/f^21/f2, the integrals ∫0dff\int_0\frac{df}{f}∫0​fdf​ and ∫0dff2\int_0\frac{df}{f^2}∫0​f2df​ diverge at low frequency.

ADEV's fix: replace "subtract the grand mean" with "adjacent differences". Step 3 showed that ADEV's equivalent kernel behaves like f2f^2f2 as f→0f\to0f→0 (sin⁡4(πfτ)␀␀∼(πfτ)4\sin^4(\pi f\tau)\sim(\pi f\tau)^4sin4(πfτ)∼(πfτ)4, divided by (πfτ)2(\pi f\tau)^2(πfτ)2, gives ∼f2\sim f^2∼f2). This f2f^2f2 high-pass tames the low-frequency divergence:

  • flicker FM (Sy∼1/fS_y\sim1/fSy​∼1/f): the integrand ∼f2⋅f−1=f\sim f^2\cdot f^{-1}=f∼f2⋅f−1=f, convergent as f→0f\to0f→0 ✓.
  • random-walk FM (Sy∼1/f2S_y\sim1/f^2Sy​∼1/f2): the integrand ∼f2⋅f−2=f0\sim f^2\cdot f^{-2}=f^0∼f2⋅f−2=f0, still convergent as f→0f\to0f→0 (a borderline case, but finite) ✓.

So ADEV is a convergent, repeatable, measurement-duration-independent well-defined quantity all the way up to random-walk FM. That is the fundamental reason David Allan proposed it in 1966 and the frequency-standards community (NIST, IEEE) adopted it as the standard:

In one sentence: the ordinary frequency variance does not converge for flicker/RW noise (it diverges the longer you collect data); ADEV uses the first difference "subtract the adjacent gate" to block the low-frequency drift, buying a stability metric that is convergent in τ\tauτ and repeatably measurable.

  • Extensions: if you also need to distinguish white PM from flicker PM, use MDEV; to ask "is a given time error bounded", use TDEV / time variance. This page focuses on the most commonly used overlapping ADEV.

Corresponding simulation figure​

lab_19 (simulations/lab_19_allan.py) generates the fractional frequency y(t)y(t)y(t) for the three FM noise types by FFT shaping, integrates it into the time error x(t)=∫y dtx(t)=\int y\,dtx(t)=∫ydt, and then estimates the overlapping Allan deviation: for each τ=mτ0\tau=m\tau_0τ=mτ0​, take the mean square of the second difference xk+2m−2xk+m+xkx_{k+2m}-2x_{k+m}+x_kxk+2m​−2xk+m​+xk​ and the square root. In the figure, solid lines are the simulated ADEV, dashed lines the theoretical slopes; the three slopes land precisely on −1/2-1/2−1/2, 000, and +1/2+1/2+1/2:

Core Python (full script: simulations/lab_19_allan.py, function overlapping_adev):

import numpy as np

def overlapping_adev(x, tau0, ms):
    """Compute the overlapping Allan deviation from time-error samples x (spacing tau0)."""
    x = np.asarray(x); N = len(x); out = []
    for m in ms:
        if N - 2 * m < 1:
            out.append(np.nan); continue
        d = x[2 * m:] - 2 * x[m:-m] + x[:-2 * m]      # second difference of the time error
        avar = np.sum(d ** 2) / (2 * (N - 2 * m) * (m * tau0) ** 2)
        out.append(np.sqrt(avar))
    return np.array(out)

The d line is the second difference xk+2m−2xk+m+xkx_{k+2m}-2x_{k+m}+x_kxk+2m​−2xk+m​+xk​ of Step 2; dividing by 2(N−2m)(mτ0)22(N-2m)(m\tau_0)^22(N−2m)(mτ0​)2 corresponds to the discrete estimate of σy2=⟨12(yˉk+1−yˉk)2⟩\sigma_y^2=\langle\tfrac12(\bar y_{k+1}-\bar y_k)^2\rangleσy2​=⟨21​(yˉ​k+1​−yˉ​k​)2⟩ (with τ=mτ0\tau=m\tau_0τ=mτ0​).

Interactive: generate your own time series and estimate ADEV yourself (statistics vs. analytic)​

The lab_19 figure above tells you the three slopes a priori. In practice, though, you only ever have one finite-length measured time series, and ADEV is a statistic estimated from that series — not an analytic curve handed down from above. The widget below moves the full "generate → estimate" pipeline into the browser, complementing the AllanDeviationExplorer on the interactive_calculator page (which plots the pure analytic slope with no randomness at all):

  • A seeded pseudo-random number generator (PRNG — meaning the same seed always reproduces the same series) generates a fractional-frequency series y[k]y[k]y[k] of length N=4096N=4096N=4096, made of slider-controlled white FM + random-walk FM, plus an optional flicker FM approximated with a simple −10-10−10dB/decade filter cascade (an honest approximation — see the note below).
  • The series is integrated into a time error x[k]=∑y[k]τ0x[k]=\sum y[k]\tau_0x[k]=∑y[k]τ0​, and the same overlapping second-difference formula from Steps 2–3 is applied to estimate ADEV directly at τ=τ0,2τ0,4τ0,…\tau=\tau_0,2\tau_0,4\tau_0,\dotsτ=τ0​,2τ0​,4τ0​,… (octaves, up to N/4N/4N/4), with ±σ/pairs\pm\sigma/\sqrt{\text{pairs}}±σ/pairs​ error bars overlaid.
  • The dashed line is the analytic closed form for the same mixture of hhh coefficients (Step 4 / the prefactor table, variances of independent processes add) — the blue points should scatter around it.
  • Click "re-seed" to draw a new seed: the small-τ\tauτ points barely move (thousands of independent pairs, statistically stable), while the large-τ\tauτ points visibly jump around (only about 4 independent pairs remain at τ=N/4\tau=N/4τ=N/4). This is exactly the lesson of this section: the "floor" or "upturn" you see at the far right of an ADEV curve can look like a definite physical feature, but if it is only supported by a handful of independent samples, those last few points carry large statistical uncertainty of their own — the fix is a longer total record, not taking the shape of the rightmost points at face value.

Estimator: overlapping ADEV σ_y²(mτ₀) = Σᵢ(x[i+2m]−2x[i+m]+x[i])² / (2·pairs·(mτ₀)²), the discrete second difference of the time error x = ∫y dt (identical formula to lab_19 / the analytic page above). Error bars use the rule-of-thumb ±σ/√pairs — a simplification (overlapping windows are correlated, so this understates the true uncertainty somewhat), but it correctly shows the qualitative point: the largest τ has few independent windows (N/τ ~ 4 at τ=N/4), so its ADEV point is noisy and jumps a lot between re-seeds, while small-τ points (thousands of pairs) are stable run to run. Flicker FM here is only an honest approximation: a cascade of 8 log-spaced one-pole (leaky-integrator) filters gives an effective PSD slope around −0.8 to −0.9 decade⁻¹ (not the exact −1 of true 1/f) over the covered band — good enough to see the τ⁰ floor bend into view, not a rigorous flicker generator. Verified in Node against a pure white-FM case (h₀=10⁻¹⁹, random-walk and flicker off): averaged over 200 reseeds the measured/theory ratio is 0.94–1.00 across all 11 octaves (worst at the largest τ, where pairs are scarcest — see below), and the fitted log–log slope of the seed-averaged curve is −0.508 (expected −1/2); a single seed (default seed 1234) already gives ratio 0.993 at the smallest τ.

Independent check of the estimator: switching the generator to pure white FM (random-walk and flicker off) with h0=10−19h_0=10^{-19}h0​=10−19 and running the same algorithm in Node over 200 re-seeds, the measured/theory ratio (against the closed form h0/2τh_0/2\tauh0​/2τ) at every octave of τ\tauτ falls in the range 0.940.940.94–1.001.001.00 (worst at the largest τ\tauτ, where pairs are scarcest — exactly the effect described above); the log–log slope fitted to the 200-seed-averaged curve is −0.508-0.508−0.508 (theory: τ−1/2\tau^{-1/2}τ−1/2), and a single run with the default seed (1234) already gives a ratio of 0.9930.9930.993 at the smallest τ\tauτ. The widget's "smallest τ measured/theory" readout is a live version of this same self-check.

Worked examples​

The two problems below follow the strict format: problem → step-by-step substitution (with units) → result → dimension check → one-line Python verification. The first practices "reading slopes off the plot"; the second demonstrates estimating ADEV from L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f) (the most useful engineering conversion).

Example 1: reading the noise type from two ADEV points and extrapolating​

Problem: an OCXO (oven-controlled crystal oscillator) measures σy(1 s)=2×10−12\sigma_y(1\,\text{s})=2\times10^{-12}σy​(1s)=2×10−12 and σy(10 s)=6.3×10−13\sigma_y(10\,\text{s})=6.3\times10^{-13}σy​(10s)=6.3×10−13. Which noise type dominates in this range? Extrapolate σy(100 s)\sigma_y(100\,\text{s})σy​(100s).

Steps:

  1. Compute the slope μ\muμ (σy∝τμ\sigma_y\propto\tau^\muσy​∝τμ):
μ=log⁡10 ⁣(σy(10)/σy(1))log⁡10(10/1)=log⁡10(6.3×10−13/2×10−12)log⁡1010=log⁡10(0.315)1≈−0.5.\mu=\frac{\log_{10}\!\big(\sigma_y(10)/\sigma_y(1)\big)}{\log_{10}(10/1)}=\frac{\log_{10}(6.3\times10^{-13}/2\times10^{-12})}{\log_{10}10}=\frac{\log_{10}(0.315)}{1}\approx-0.5.μ=log10​(10/1)log10​(σy​(10)/σy​(1))​=log10​10log10​(6.3×10−13/2×10−12)​=1log10​(0.315)​≈−0.5.
  1. Consulting the Step-4 table: μ=−1/2\mu=-1/2μ=−1/2 ⇒ white FM dominates (Sy∼f0S_y\sim f^0Sy​∼f0, equivalently Sϕ∼1/f2S_\phi\sim1/f^2Sϕ​∼1/f2).
  2. Extrapolate to τ=100 s\tau=100\,\text{s}τ=100s (still white FM, τ−1/2\tau^{-1/2}τ−1/2):
σy(100)=σy(1)×(100)−1/2=2×10−12×110=2×10−13.\sigma_y(100)=\sigma_y(1)\times(100)^{-1/2}=2\times10^{-12}\times\frac{1}{10}=2\times10^{-13}.σy​(100)=σy​(1)×(100)−1/2=2×10−12×101​=2×10−13.

Result: white FM dominates; σy(100 s)≈2×10−13\sigma_y(100\,\text{s})\approx2\times10^{-13}σy​(100s)≈2×10−13.

Dimension check: σy\sigma_yσy​ is dimensionless throughout (fractional frequency); the slope μ\muμ is a ratio of logs of two dimensionless quantities, hence dimensionless ✓.

import numpy as np
mu = np.log10(6.3e-13/2e-12)/np.log10(10)          # -> -0.50  => white FM
adev_100 = 2e-12*(100/1)**mu
print(round(mu,2), f"{adev_100:.2e}")              # -> -0.5  2.00e-13

Problem: a 5 GHz oscillator measures L(1 MHz)=−100 dBc/Hz\mathcal{L}(1\,\text{MHz})=-100\,\text{dBc/Hz}L(1MHz)=−100dBc/Hz in the 1/f² region (the white-FM segment). Estimate how σy(τ)\sigma_y(\tau)σy​(τ) scales with τ\tauτ, and give the numerical value of σy(1 ms)\sigma_y(1\,\text{ms})σy​(1ms). Uses the setup of canonical Example C (f0=5 GHzf_0=5\,\text{GHz}f0​=5GHz).

Steps:

  1. dBc/Hz → linear L\mathcal{L}L: L(1 MHz)=10−100/10=10−10 rad2/Hz\mathcal{L}(1\,\text{MHz})=10^{-100/10}=10^{-10}\,\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}L(1MHz)=10−100/10=10−10rad2/Hz (single-sided).

Substituting f=106f=10^6f=106: h−2=Sϕ(106)⋅(106)2=2×10−10×1012=2×102=200 rad2 Hzh_{-2}=S_\phi(10^6)\cdot(10^6)^2=2\times10^{-10}\times10^{12}=2\times10^{2}=200\,\text{rad}^2\,\text{Hz}h−2​=Sϕ​(106)⋅(106)2=2×10−10×1012=2×102=200rad2Hz.

Convert to SyS_ySy​: Sy(f)=f2f02Sϕ=f2f02⋅h−2f2=h−2f02≡h0S_y(f)=\dfrac{f^2}{f_0^2}S_\phi=\dfrac{f^2}{f_0^2}\cdot\dfrac{h_{-2}}{f^2}=\dfrac{h_{-2}}{f_0^2}\equiv h_0Sy​(f)=f02​f2​Sϕ​=f02​f2​⋅f2h−2​​=f02​h−2​​≡h0​ (white indeed — independent of fff). h0=200(5×109)2=2002.5×1019=8.0×10−18 Hz−1h_0=\dfrac{200}{(5\times10^9)^2}=\dfrac{200}{2.5\times10^{19}}=8.0\times10^{-18}\,\text{Hz}^{-1}h0​=(5×109)2200​=2.5×1019200​=8.0×10−18Hz−1.

σy2(τ)=h02τ⟹σy(τ)=h02τ.\sigma_y^2(\tau)=\frac{h_0}{2\tau}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\sigma_y(\tau)=\sqrt{\frac{h_0}{2\tau}}.σy2​(τ)=2τh0​​⟹σy​(τ)=2τh0​​​.
  1. Substituting τ=10−3 s\tau=10^{-3}\,\text{s}τ=10−3s: σy2=8.0×10−182×10−3=4.0×10−15\sigma_y^2=\dfrac{8.0\times10^{-18}}{2\times10^{-3}}=4.0\times10^{-15}σy2​=2×10−38.0×10−18​=4.0×10−15, σy=6.3×10−8\sigma_y=6.3\times10^{-8}σy​=6.3×10−8.

Result: SyS_ySy​ is white with h0=8.0×10−18 Hz−1h_0=8.0\times10^{-18}\,\text{Hz}^{-1}h0​=8.0×10−18Hz−1; σy(τ)=h0/2τ∝τ−1/2\sigma_y(\tau)=\sqrt{h_0/2\tau}\propto\tau^{-1/2}σy​(τ)=h0​/2τ​∝τ−1/2 (consistent with white FM); σy(1 ms)≈6.3×10−8\sigma_y(1\,\text{ms})\approx6.3\times10^{-8}σy​(1ms)≈6.3×10−8.

Dimension check: h0h_0h0​ has units Hz−1=s\text{Hz}^{-1}=\text{s}Hz−1=s; h0/τh_0/\tauh0​/τ is dimensionless; the square root remains dimensionless → σy\sigma_yσy​ dimensionless ✓. The slope σy∝τ−1/2\sigma_y\propto\tau^{-1/2}σy​∝τ−1/2 matches the white-FM row of the table ✓.

Feel for the numbers: 6.3×10−86.3\times10^{-8}6.3×10−8 looks large at 1 ms, but a free-running 5 GHz oscillator does drift away a lot of phase within 1 ms (which is exactly why a PLL/CDR is used to pin the long-term frequency; see serdes_clocking_connection). Stretch τ\tauτ to 1 s and σy\sigma_yσy​ drops by another factor 1000≈31.6\sqrt{1000}\approx31.61000​≈31.6 to ∼2×10−9\sim2\times10^{-9}∼2×10−9.

import numpy as np
f0, L_dbc, foff = 5e9, -100.0, 1e6
S_phi = 2*10**(L_dbc/10)                 # rad^2/Hz at foff (small-angle L≈½S_φ)
h_2   = S_phi*foff**2                     # S_phi = h_2/f^2  => h_2
h0    = h_2/f0**2                         # S_y = h0 (white FM)
adev  = lambda tau: np.sqrt(h0/(2*tau))
print(f"{h0:.1e}", f"{adev(1e-3):.1e}")  # -> 8.0e-18  6.3e-08

(The white-FM closed form σy2=h0/2τ\sigma_y^2=h_0/2\tauσy2​=h0​/2τ is a standard frequency-metrology result — the next section derives it fully in-house using I2=π/4I_2=\pi/4I2​=π/4, and lab_19 has been extended to verify the absolute level as well, not just the slope.)

The complete prefactor table: the flicker-FM floor constant σy2=2ln⁡2⋅h−1\sigma_y^2=2\ln 2\cdot h_{-1}σy2​=2ln2⋅h−1​​

The Step-4 slope table only answers "σy∝τμ\sigma_y\propto\tau^\muσy​∝τμ" — it says nothing about the absolute level. What engineering actually needs is: given the power-law coefficients of SyS_ySy​, the exact numerical value of each segment of the ADEV curve — above all, how high the flicker-FM floor sits, the level that "no amount of averaging gets you below". This section evaluates the Step-3 integral for each of the five power laws one by one: the centerpiece is the flicker-FM floor constant, which turns out to be a beautiful ln⁡2\ln 2ln2; white FM and RW FM fall to the same trick along the way; and the two PM types will show us "why a high-frequency cutoff fhf_hfh​ is unavoidable".

Notation: the power-law coefficients hαh_\alphahα​ (standard IEEE 1139 notation)​

The frequency-metrology standards write SyS_ySy​ as a power-law superposition:

Sy(f)=∑α=−2+2hαfα.S_y(f)=\sum_{\alpha=-2}^{+2}h_\alpha f^{\alpha}.Sy​(f)=α=−2∑+2​hα​fα.

SyS_ySy​ has units 1/Hz1/\text{Hz}1/Hz, so hαh_\alphahα​ has units Hz−(α+1)\text{Hz}^{-(\alpha+1)}Hz−(α+1): h+2h_{+2}h+2​ is Hz−3\text{Hz}^{-3}Hz−3, h+1h_{+1}h+1​ is Hz−2\text{Hz}^{-2}Hz−2, h0h_0h0​ is Hz−1=s\text{Hz}^{-1}=\text{s}Hz−1=s, h−1h_{-1}h−1​ is dimensionless, h−2h_{-2}h−2​ is Hz\text{Hz}Hz.

Notation warning: the hαh_\alphahα​ always attach to SyS_ySy​ (the standard IEEE 1139 usage). In Example 2 above we casually wrote the 1/f21/f^21/f2 coefficient of SϕS_\phiSϕ​ as h−2h_{-2}h−2​ — that is the SϕS_\phiSϕ​-side coefficient, not the same object as the RW-FM h−2h_{-2}h−2​ here (which lives on the SyS_ySy​ side, with units Hz). From this section on, SϕS_\phiSϕ​-side coefficients carry a superscript ϕ\phiϕ: the white-FM segment is written Sϕ=h−2ϕ/f2S_\phi=h^{\phi}_{-2}/f^2Sϕ​=h−2ϕ​/f2 (with h−2ϕh^{\phi}_{-2}h−2ϕ​ in rad2⋅Hz\text{rad}^2\cdot\text{Hz}rad2⋅Hz).

The general formula: one substitution covers all five rows​

Substitute Sy=hαfαS_y=h_\alpha f^\alphaSy​=hα​fα into the Step-3 integral and change variables u=πfτu=\pi f\tauu=πfτ (dimensionless; f=u/(πτ)f=u/(\pi\tau)f=u/(πτ), df=du/(πτ)df=du/(\pi\tau)df=du/(πτ), fα=uα/(πτ)αf^\alpha=u^\alpha/(\pi\tau)^\alphafα=uα/(πτ)α):

σy2(τ)=2∫0∞hαfα sin⁡4(πfτ)(πfτ)2 df=2 hα(πτ)α+1 I2−α,Ik≡∫0∞sin⁡4uuk du.\sigma_y^2(\tau)=2\int_0^{\infty}h_\alpha f^{\alpha}\,\frac{\sin^4(\pi f\tau)}{(\pi f\tau)^2}\,df =\frac{2\,h_\alpha}{(\pi\tau)^{\alpha+1}}\,I_{2-\alpha}, \qquad I_k\equiv\int_0^{\infty}\frac{\sin^4 u}{u^{k}}\,du.σy2​(τ)=2∫0∞​hα​fα(πfτ)2sin4(πfτ)​df=(πτ)α+12hα​​I2−α​,Ik​≡∫0∞​uksin4u​du.
  • Step by step: the integrand =hαuα(πτ)α⋅sin⁡4uu2⋅duπτ=hα (πτ)−(α+1) sin⁡4uu2−α du=h_\alpha\dfrac{u^\alpha}{(\pi\tau)^\alpha}\cdot\dfrac{\sin^4u}{u^2}\cdot\dfrac{du}{\pi\tau}=h_\alpha\,(\pi\tau)^{-(\alpha+1)}\,\dfrac{\sin^4u}{u^{2-\alpha}}\,du=hα​(πτ)αuα​⋅u2sin4u​⋅πτdu​=hα​(πτ)−(α+1)u2−αsin4u​du; pull out the constants and the result follows.
  • The slope table comes out for free: σy2∝τ−(α+1)\sigma_y^2\propto\tau^{-(\alpha+1)}σy2​∝τ−(α+1) — α=0⇒τ−1\alpha=0\Rightarrow\tau^{-1}α=0⇒τ−1 (white FM), α=−1⇒τ0\alpha=-1\Rightarrow\tau^{0}α=−1⇒τ0 (floor), α=−2⇒τ+1\alpha=-2\Rightarrow\tau^{+1}α=−2⇒τ+1 (RW FM), consistent with the Step-4 table ✓. All that remains is to evaluate the pure numbers IkI_kIk​.
  • Convergence (important): as u→0u\to0u→0 the integrand ∼u4−k\sim u^{4-k}∼u4−k (k=2−α≤4k=2-\alpha\le4k=2−α≤4, integrable for all α≥−2\alpha\ge-2α≥−2 ✓); as u→∞u\to\inftyu→∞ it goes ∼u−k\sim u^{-k}∼u−k, requiring k>1k>1k>1, i.e. α<1\alpha<1α<1. For α=+1,+2\alpha=+1,+2α=+1,+2 (the two PM types) the integral diverges at the high-frequency end — physically: the ADEV of PM noise depends on how high a frequency the measurement system can see, so a high-frequency cutoff fhf_hfh​ (Hz) must be introduced, truncating at uh=πfhτu_h=\pi f_h\tauuh​=πfh​τ. This is the deeper reason why the two PM rows of the Step-4 table cannot do without fhf_hfh​.
  • Unit check: hαh_\alphahα​ is Hz−(α+1)\text{Hz}^{-(\alpha+1)}Hz−(α+1), (πτ)−(α+1)(\pi\tau)^{-(\alpha+1)}(πτ)−(α+1) is Hz+(α+1)\text{Hz}^{+(\alpha+1)}Hz+(α+1), IkI_kIk​ is a pure number ⇒ σy2\sigma_y^2σy2​ dimensionless ✓.

Flicker FM (α=−1\alpha=-1α=−1): proving I3=ln⁡2I_3=\ln 2I3​=ln2​

For α=−1\alpha=-1α=−1 we get (πτ)α+1=(πτ)0=1(\pi\tau)^{\alpha+1}=(\pi\tau)^{0}=1(πτ)α+1=(π␀τ)0=1 — τ\tauτ disappears entirely at the very first step; the "τ\tauτ-independence" of the floor is established right here, before evaluating any integral:

σy2(τ)=2 h−1 I3=2 h−1∫0∞sin⁡4uu3 du.\sigma_y^2(\tau)=2\,h_{-1}\,I_3=2\,h_{-1}\int_0^{\infty}\frac{\sin^4u}{u^3}\,du.σy2​(τ)=2h−1​I3​=2h−1​∫0∞​u3sin4u​du.

All that is left is the pure number I3I_3I3​. Four sub-steps below, no jumps.

Step (i): power-reduce sin⁡4\sin^4sin4 into harmonics. Square sin⁡2u=12(1−cos⁡2u)\sin^2u=\tfrac12(1-\cos2u)sin2u=21​(1−cos2u), then use cos⁡22u=12(1+cos⁡4u)\cos^2 2u=\tfrac12(1+\cos4u)cos22u=21​(1+cos4u):

sin⁡4u=(1−cos⁡2u)24=1−2cos⁡2u+cos⁡22u4=3−4cos⁡2u+cos⁡4u8=4(1−cos⁡2u)−(1−cos⁡4u)8.\sin^4u=\frac{(1-\cos2u)^2}{4}=\frac{1-2\cos2u+\cos^2 2u}{4}=\frac{3-4\cos2u+\cos4u}{8}=\frac{4(1-\cos2u)-(1-\cos4u)}{8}.sin4u=4(1−cos2u)2​=41−2cos2u+cos22u​=83−4cos2u+cos4u​=84(1−cos2u)−(1−cos4u)​.

Check the last equality: 4−4cos⁡2u−1+cos⁡4u=3−4cos⁡2u+cos⁡4u4-4\cos2u-1+\cos4u=3-4\cos2u+\cos4u4−4cos2u−1+cos4u=3−4cos2u+cos4u ✓. Small-uuu check: 1−cos⁡(au)=a2u22−a4u424+…1-\cos(au)=\tfrac{a^2u^2}{2}-\tfrac{a^4u^4}{24}+\dots1−cos(au)=2a2u2​−24a4u4​+…; the u2u^2u2 coefficient 4⋅42−162=8−8=04\cdot\tfrac{4}{2}-\tfrac{16}{2}=8-8=04⋅24​−216​=8−8=0 cancels, and the u4u^4u4 term −4⋅1624+25624=8-4\cdot\tfrac{16}{24}+\tfrac{256}{24}=8−4⋅2416​+24256​=8 gives the combination ≈8u4=8sin⁡4u\approx8u^4=8\sin^4u≈8u4=8sin4u ✓ (sin⁡4u≈u4\sin^4u\approx u^4sin4u≈u4).

Step (ii): why we must group into "(1−cos⁡)(1-\cos)(1−cos) combinations" and may not split. If you integrate 3−4cos⁡2u+cos⁡4u3-4\cos2u+\cos4u3−4cos2u+cos4u against u−3u^{-3}u−3 term by term, each piece 1−cos⁡(au)u3≈a22u\dfrac{1-\cos(au)}{u^3}\approx\dfrac{a^2}{2u}u31−cos(au)​≈2ua2​ diverges logarithmically as u→0u\to0u→0; only in the combination does the 1/u1/u1/u coefficient 4⋅222−422=04\cdot\tfrac{2^2}{2}-\tfrac{4^2}{2}=04⋅222​−242​=0 cancel exactly, making the whole thing integrable (low end sin⁡4u/u3␀␀∼u→0\sin^4u/u^3\sim u\to0sin4u/u3∼u→0, high end ≤1/u3\le1/u^3≤1/u3 ✓). So below we treat it as a whole and never split — this "individually divergent, finite in combination" structure is exactly the usual temperament of 1/f1/f1/f noise (compare Step 5: the standard variance diverges while the differenced combination converges).

Step (iii): integrate by parts twice, lowering u−3u^{-3}u−3 to u−1u^{-1}u−1. Write g(u)≡8sin⁡4u=3−4cos⁡2u+cos⁡4ug(u)\equiv8\sin^4u=3-4\cos2u+\cos4ug(u)≡8sin4u=3−4cos2u+cos4u, so I3=18∫0∞g(u) u−3duI_3=\tfrac18\int_0^\infty g(u)\,u^{-3}duI3​=81​∫0∞​g(u)u−3du.

First integration by parts (u−3du=d(−12u2)u^{-3}du=d(-\tfrac{1}{2u^2})u−3du=d(−2u21​)):

∫0∞g(u)u3 du=[−g(u)2u2]0∞+12∫0∞g′(u)u2 du,g′(u)=8sin⁡2u−4sin⁡4u.\int_0^{\infty}\frac{g(u)}{u^3}\,du=\Big[-\frac{g(u)}{2u^2}\Big]_0^{\infty}+\frac12\int_0^{\infty}\frac{g'(u)}{u^2}\,du, \qquad g'(u)=8\sin2u-4\sin4u.∫0∞​u3g(u)​du=[−2u2g(u)​]0∞​+21​∫0∞​u2g′(u)​du,g′(u)=8sin2u−4sin4u.

Boundary terms: as u→∞u\to\inftyu→∞, ∣g∣≤8\lvert g\rvert\le8∣g∣≤8 ⇒ g/u2→0g/u^2\to0g/u2→0; as u→0u\to0u→0, g≈8u4g\approx8u^4g≈8u4 ⇒ g/(2u2)≈4u2→0g/(2u^2)\approx4u^2\to0g/(2u2)≈4u2→0 ✓ both ends vanish.

Second integration by parts (u−2du=d(−u−1)u^{-2}du=d(-u^{-1})u−2du=d(−u−1)):

∫0∞g′(u)u2 du=[−g′(u)u]0∞+∫0∞g′′(u)u du,g′′(u)=16cos⁡2u−16cos⁡4u.\int_0^{\infty}\frac{g'(u)}{u^2}\,du=\Big[-\frac{g'(u)}{u}\Big]_0^{\infty}+\int_0^{\infty}\frac{g''(u)}{u}\,du, \qquad g''(u)=16\cos2u-16\cos4u.∫0∞​u2g′(u)​du=[−ug′(u)​]0∞​+∫0∞​ug′′(u)​du,g′′(u)=16cos2u−16cos4u.

Boundary terms: at the ∞\infty∞ end g′g'g′ is bounded ⇒ g′/u→0g'/u\to0g′/u→0; at the 000 end g′=8sin⁡2u−4sin⁡4u=(16u−16u)+O(u3)=32u3+O(u5)g'=8\sin2u-4\sin4u=(16u-16u)+O(u^3)=32u^3+O(u^5)g′=8sin2u−4sin4u=(16u−16u)+O(u3)=32u3+O(u5) ⇒ g′/u≈32u2→0g'/u\approx32u^2\to0g′/u≈32u2→0 ✓. Combining:

I3=18⋅12∫0∞16(cos⁡2u−cos⁡4u)u du=∫0∞cos⁡2u−cos⁡4uu du.I_3=\frac18\cdot\frac12\int_0^{\infty}\frac{16(\cos2u-\cos4u)}{u}\,du=\int_0^{\infty}\frac{\cos2u-\cos4u}{u}\,du.I3​=81​⋅21​∫0∞​u16(cos2u−cos4u)​du=∫0∞​ucos2u−cos4u​du.

Step (iv): a Frullani-type cosine integral → ln⁡2\ln2ln2. Each term alone diverges as u→0u\to0u→0 (∫du/u\int du/u∫du/u), but the combination is integrable (cos⁡2u−cos⁡4u=6u2+O(u4)\cos2u-\cos4u=6u^2+O(u^4)cos2u−cos4u=6u2+O(u4), integrand ∼6u→0\sim6u\to0∼6u→0). Take a lower limit ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 and substitute v=2uv=2uv=2u and v=4uv=4uv=4u in the two terms respectively:

∫ε∞cos⁡2u−cos⁡4uu du=∫2ε∞cos⁡vv dv−∫4ε∞cos⁡vv dv=∫2ε4εcos⁡vv dv.\int_{\varepsilon}^{\infty}\frac{\cos2u-\cos4u}{u}\,du=\int_{2\varepsilon}^{\infty}\frac{\cos v}{v}\,dv-\int_{4\varepsilon}^{\infty}\frac{\cos v}{v}\,dv=\int_{2\varepsilon}^{4\varepsilon}\frac{\cos v}{v}\,dv.∫ε∞​ucos2u−cos4u​du=∫2ε∞​vcosv​dv−∫4ε∞​vcosv​dv=∫2ε4ε​vcosv​dv.

(At the ∞\infty∞ end each integral converges conditionally — Dirichlet's test — and the identical tails cancel on subtraction, leaving only the sliver [2ε,4ε][2\varepsilon,4\varepsilon][2ε,4ε].) On that sliver ∣cos⁡v−1∣≤v2/2\lvert\cos v-1\rvert\le v^2/2∣cosv−1∣≤v2/2:

∫2ε4εcos⁡vv dv=∫2ε4εdvv+O(ε2)=ln⁡4ε2ε+O(ε2) → ε→0  ln⁡2.\int_{2\varepsilon}^{4\varepsilon}\frac{\cos v}{v}\,dv=\int_{2\varepsilon}^{4\varepsilon}\frac{dv}{v}+O(\varepsilon^2)=\ln\frac{4\varepsilon}{2\varepsilon}+O(\varepsilon^2)\ \xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon\to0\ }\ \ln2.∫2ε4ε​vcosv​dv=∫2ε4ε​vdv​+O(ε2)=ln2ε4ε​+O(ε2)  ε→0 ​ ln2.

Therefore:

 I3=∫0∞sin⁡4uu3 du=ln⁡2⟹σy2(τ)=2ln⁡2⋅h−1 (independent of τ),σy,floor=2ln⁡2⋅h−1≈1.1774 h−1 \boxed{\ I_3=\int_0^{\infty}\frac{\sin^4u}{u^3}\,du=\ln2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sigma_y^2(\tau)=2\ln2\cdot h_{-1}\ (\text{independent of }\tau),\quad \sigma_{y,\text{floor}}=\sqrt{2\ln2\cdot h_{-1}}\approx1.1774\,\sqrt{h_{-1}}\ } I3​=∫0∞​u3sin4u​du=ln2⟹σy2​(τ)=2ln2⋅h−1​ (independent of τ),σy,floor​=2ln2⋅h−1​​≈1.1774h−1​​ ​

Physical intuition: ln⁡2=ln⁡42\ln2=\ln\frac{4}{2}ln2=ln24​ is the log of the frequency ratio of the two harmonics 2u2u2u and 4u4u4u produced by the power reduction. A 1/f1/f1/f process contributes equal power per octave; the ADEV band-pass kernel, on a log-frequency axis, is a window of fixed shape that merely slides with τ\tauτ (weighted by Sy∼1/fS_y\sim1/fSy​∼1/f, the contribution density per decade is ∝sin⁡4u/u2\propto\sin^4u/u^2∝sin4u/u2, peaking at tan⁡u=2u\tan u=2utanu=2u, i.e. u≈1.17u\approx1.17u≈1.17, f≈0.37/τf\approx0.37/\tauf≈0.37/τ) — the window slides without changing shape, so the "number of octaves" it sees does not depend on τ\tauτ, and the integral is a constant. That is the frequency-domain picture of why the flicker floor is "τ\tauτ-independent".

Numerical verification (scipy.integrate.quad up to 200π200\pi200π plus the analytic ⟨sin⁡4⟩=3/8\langle\sin^4\rangle=3/8⟨sin4⟩=3/8 tail correction; printed by lab_19):

import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import quad
U = 200*np.pi
I3, _ = quad(lambda u: np.sin(u)**4/u**3, 0, U, limit=4000)
I3 += (3/8)/(2*U**2)                  # tail ∫_U^∞ (3/8)/u^3 du
print(f"{I3:.4f} {np.log(2):.4f}")    # -> 0.6931 0.6931

Factor-2/4 bookkeeping (the origin of every 2 and 4 in this section, settled once and for all):

  • The leading 2 in σy2=2ln⁡2⋅h−1\sigma_y^2=2\ln2\cdot h_{-1}σy2​=2ln2⋅h−1​: from the Step-3 kernel ∣H∣2=2sin⁡4u/u2\lvert H\rvert^2=2\sin^4u/u^2∣H∣2=2sin4u/u2 (the definition's 12\tfrac1221​ × the adjacent-difference 4sin⁡24\sin^24sin2) — this is ADEV mathematics, and has nothing to do with the phase-noise SSB /2/2/2-vs-/4/4/4 bookkeeping.
  • The 2 and 4 in cos⁡2u\cos2ucos2u and cos⁡4u\cos4ucos4u: the second and fourth harmonics from power-reducing sin⁡4\sin^4sin4; ln⁡2=ln⁡(4/2)\ln2=\ln(4/2)ln2=ln(4/2) is precisely their frequency ratio.
  • The 2 in the white-FM denominator h0/(2τ)h_0/(2\tau)h0​/(2τ): 2⋅I2π=2⋅π/4π=122\cdot\frac{I_2}{\pi}=2\cdot\frac{\pi/4}{\pi}=\frac122⋅πI2​​=2⋅ππ/4​=21​ — again ADEV mathematics, not SSB bookkeeping.
  • The 4π24\pi^24π2 in the denominator of h−2ϕh^{\phi}_{-2}h−2ϕ​ in Example 3 below: from (2πf)2(2\pi f)^2(2πf)2, purely the rad ↔ Hz conversion.
  • The 4 in the denominator of τknee\tau_{knee}τknee​ in Example 3: =2×2=2\times2=2×2 (the 2 of h0/2τh_0/\mathbf{2}\tauh0​/2τ × the 2 of 2ln⁡2\mathbf{2}\ln22ln2).
  • The genuine SSB /2/2/2-vs-/4/4/4 convention appears only when "converting SϕS_\phiSϕ​ into a dBc/Hz report" (flagged in Example 3, Step 1).

The same trick takes down white FM and RW FM (and the fhf_hfh​ of the two PM rows)​

White FM (α=0\alpha=0α=0): σy2=2h0πτI2\sigma_y^2=\dfrac{2h_0}{\pi\tau}I_2σy2​=πτ2h0​​I2​. I2I_2I2​ needs only one integration by parts (the boundary terms again vanish at both ends: sin⁡4u/u∼u3→0\sin^4u/u\sim u^3\to0sin4u/u∼u3→0 and ≤1/u→0\le1/u\to0≤1/u→0):

I2=∫0∞sin⁡4uu2 du=[−sin⁡4uu]0∞+∫0∞4sin⁡3ucos⁡uu du=∫0∞sin⁡2u−12sin⁡4uu du=π2−12⋅π2=π4.I_2=\int_0^{\infty}\frac{\sin^4u}{u^2}\,du=\Big[-\frac{\sin^4u}{u}\Big]_0^{\infty}+\int_0^{\infty}\frac{4\sin^3u\cos u}{u}\,du=\int_0^{\infty}\frac{\sin2u-\tfrac12\sin4u}{u}\,du=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac12\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}=\frac{\pi}{4}.I2​=∫0∞​u2sin4u​du=[−usin4u​]0∞​+∫0∞​u4sin3ucosu​du=∫0∞​usin2u−21​sin4u​du=2π​−21​⋅2π​=4π​.

(In the middle we used 4sin⁡3ucos⁡u=2sin⁡2usin⁡2u=sin⁡2u(1−cos⁡2u)=sin⁡2u−12sin⁡4u4\sin^3u\cos u=2\sin2u\sin^2u=\sin2u(1-\cos2u)=\sin2u-\tfrac12\sin4u4sin3ucosu=2sin2usin2u=sin2u(1−cos2u)=sin2u−21​sin4u, plus the Dirichlet integral ∫0∞sin⁡(au)udu=π2\int_0^\infty\frac{\sin(au)}{u}du=\frac{\pi}{2}∫0∞​usin(au)​du=2π​, a>0a>0a>0.) σy2(τ)=2h0πτ⋅π4=h02τ.\sigma_y^2(\tau)=\frac{2h_0}{\pi\tau}\cdot\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{h_0}{2\tau}.σy2​(τ)=πτ2h0​​⋅4π​=2τh0​​.

Example 3: computing the flicker floor from the canonical 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner (with units)​

Problem: the canonical oscillator (f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, Si=10−24 A2/HzS_i=10^{-24}\ \text{A}^2/\text{Hz}Si​=10−24 A2/Hz), with waveform symmetrized so that c0=0.04c_0=0.04c0​=0.04; Example F of flicker_noise_upconversion gives the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner fc=3.2f_c=3.2fc​=3.2 kHz. Find the flicker-FM floor σy,floor\sigma_{y,\text{floor}}σy,floor​ and the τknee\tau_{knee}τknee​ where the white-FM segment crosses the floor.

Step 1 (the physical SϕS_\phiSϕ​ of the white-FM segment): the time-domain-clean derivation (see the factor-of-2 note in white_noise_to_phase_noise) gives the single-sided

Sϕ(f)=Γrms2qmax2⋅Si(2πf)2=h−2ϕf2,h−2ϕ=Γrms2 Si4π2 qmax2=0.25×10−244π2×10−24=6.33×10−3 rad2⋅Hz.S_\phi(f)=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{S_i}{(2\pi f)^2}=\frac{h^{\phi}_{-2}}{f^2}, \qquad h^{\phi}_{-2}=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2\,S_i}{4\pi^2\,q_{max}^2}=\frac{0.25\times10^{-24}}{4\pi^2\times10^{-24}}=6.33\times10^{-3}\ \text{rad}^2\cdot\text{Hz}.Sϕ​(f)=qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅(2πf)2Si​​=f2h−2ϕ​​,h−2ϕ​=4π2qmax2​Γrms2​Si​​=4π2×10−240.25×10−24​=6.33×10−3 rad2⋅Hz.
  • Unit check: A2/Hz÷C2=(C/s)2/(Hz⋅C2)=Hz2/Hz=Hz\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}\div\text{C}^2=(\text{C/s})^2/(\text{Hz}\cdot\text{C}^2)=\text{Hz}^2/\text{Hz}=\text{Hz}A2/Hz÷C2=(C/s)2/(Hz⋅C2)=Hz2/Hz=Hz, times the dimensionless Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​ gives rad2⋅Hz\text{rad}^2\cdot\text{Hz}rad2⋅Hz ✓ (the 4π24\pi^24π2 in the denominator comes from (2πf)2(2\pi f)^2(2πf)2 — a rad↔Hz conversion, not a noise-bookkeeping convention).
  • Convention flag (every single time): this is the physical single-sided SϕS_\phiSϕ​. When converted into a dBc/Hz report: the time-domain /2/2/2 convention (L=Sϕ/2\mathcal{L}=S_\phi/2L=Sϕ​/2) gives L(1 MHz)=−145.0\mathcal{L}(1\,\text{MHz})=-145.0L(1MHz)=−145.0 dBc/Hz, while the SSB /4/4/4 accounting of [P1] Eq.(21) gives −148.0-148.0−148.0 dBc/Hz (a 3 dB difference; canonical Example B). ADEV consumes only the physical SϕS_\phiSϕ​, so this example corresponds to the −145-145−145 reading; if you mistakenly invert −148-148−148 as Sϕ/2S_\phi/2Sϕ​/2, your h−2ϕh^{\phi}_{-2}h−2ϕ​ comes out 2× too small and the floor 2\sqrt22​ too low (−1.5-1.5−1.5 dB).

Step 2 (flicker segment → h−1h_{-1}h−1​): below the corner, SϕS_\phiSϕ​ steepens to 1/f31/f^31/f3, continuous with the white-FM segment at fcf_cfc​: Sϕ=h−2ϕ fcf3S_\phi=\dfrac{h^{\phi}_{-2}\,f_c}{f^3}Sϕ​=f3h−2ϕ​fc​​ (f<fcf<f_cf<fc​). Converting to SyS_ySy​ (the Step-1 adapter):

Sy(f)=f2f02 Sϕ=h−2ϕ fcf02⋅1f≡h−1f,h−1=h−2ϕ fcf02=6.33×10−3×3.2×103(5×109)2=8.11×10−19.S_y(f)=\frac{f^2}{f_0^2}\,S_\phi=\frac{h^{\phi}_{-2}\,f_c}{f_0^2}\cdot\frac1f\equiv\frac{h_{-1}}{f}, \qquad h_{-1}=\frac{h^{\phi}_{-2}\,f_c}{f_0^2}=\frac{6.33\times10^{-3}\times3.2\times10^{3}}{(5\times10^{9})^2}=8.11\times10^{-19}.Sy​(f)=f02​f2​Sϕ​=f02​h−2ϕ​fc​​⋅f1​≡fh−1​​,h−1​=f02​h−2ϕ​fc​​=(5×109)26.33×10−3×3.2×103​=8.11×10−19.
  • Unit check: rad2⋅Hz×Hz÷Hz2=\text{rad}^2\cdot\text{Hz}\times\text{Hz}\div\text{Hz}^2=rad2⋅Hz×Hz÷Hz2= dimensionless ✓ (h−1h_{-1}h−1​ should be dimensionless).
  • Worth noting: h−1=h0 fch_{-1}=h_0\,f_ch−1​=h0​fc​, where h0=h−2ϕ/f02=2.53×10−22 Hz−1h_0=h^{\phi}_{-2}/f_0^2=2.53\times10^{-22}\ \text{Hz}^{-1}h0​=h−2ϕ​/f02​=2.53×10−22 Hz−1 is the white-FM level — the flicker coefficient is just "white-FM level × corner frequency".

Step 3 (the floor):

σy,floor=2ln⁡2⋅h−1=1.3863×8.11×10−19=1.124×10−18=1.06×10−9.\sigma_{y,\text{floor}}=\sqrt{2\ln2\cdot h_{-1}}=\sqrt{1.3863\times8.11\times10^{-19}}=\sqrt{1.124\times10^{-18}}=1.06\times10^{-9}.σy,floor​=2ln2⋅h−1​​=1.3863×8.11×10−19​=1.124×10−18​=1.06×10−9.

Result: the floor is ≈1.06×10−9\approx1.06\times10^{-9}≈1.06×10−9, about 1.1 ppb — in frequency terms: σyf0=1.06×10−9×5×109=5.3\sigma_y f_0=1.06\times10^{-9}\times5\times10^{9}=5.3σy​f0​=1.06×10−9×5×109=5.3 Hz. No matter how long you average, the two-sample frequency instability of this free-running oscillator is stuck at about 5.3 Hz — that is the engineering meaning of the flicker floor.

Step 4 (the knee: where the white-FM segment hits the floor): set h0/(2τ)=2ln⁡2⋅h−1h_0/(2\tau)=2\ln2\cdot h_{-1}h0​/(2τ)=2ln2⋅h−1​ and use h−1=h0fch_{-1}=h_0f_ch−1​=h0​fc​:

τknee=h04ln⁡2⋅h−1=14ln⁡2⋅fc=0.3607fc=0.36073200 Hz=113 μs.\tau_{knee}=\frac{h_0}{4\ln2\cdot h_{-1}}=\frac{1}{4\ln2\cdot f_c}=\frac{0.3607}{f_c}=\frac{0.3607}{3200\ \text{Hz}}=113\ \mu\text{s}.τknee​=4ln2⋅h−1​h0​​=4ln2⋅fc​1​=fc​0.3607​=3200 Hz0.3607​=113 μs.

(The 4 in the denominator =2×2=2\times2=2×2: the 2 of h0/2τh_0/\mathbf{2}\tauh0​/2τ × the 2 of 2ln⁡2\mathbf{2}\ln22ln2, both ADEV mathematics.) For τ\tauτ shorter than 113 μs white FM dominates (the τ−1/2\tau^{-1/2}τ−1/2 descent); beyond it you sit on the floor. Rule of thumb: τknee≈0.36/fc\tau_{knee}\approx0.36/f_cτknee​≈0.36/fc​.

Contrast (asymmetric waveform): Example E's c0=0.4c_0=0.4c0​=0.4 gives fc=320f_c=320fc​=320 kHz ⇒ h−1=8.11×10−17h_{-1}=8.11\times10^{-17}h−1​=8.11×10−17, floor =1.06×10−8=1.06\times10^{-8}=1.06×10−8. The corner is 100× higher, the floor only 10× higher (the  \sqrt{\ } ​), and the knee shrinks to 1.13 μs. Because fc∝c02f_c\propto c_0^2fc​∝c02​ ([P1] Eq.(24)) while the floor ∝h−1∝fc\propto\sqrt{h_{-1}}\propto\sqrt{f_c}∝h−1​​∝fc​​, we get floor ∝c0\propto c_0∝c0​: waveform symmetrization does not just suppress close-in phase noise — it pulls the long-term-stability floor down linearly in c0c_0c0​.

Dimension check (throughout): h−1h_{-1}h−1​ dimensionless → 2ln⁡2 h−12\ln2\,h_{-1}2ln2h−1​ dimensionless → the square root still dimensionless (fractional frequency) ✓; τknee=h0/(4ln⁡2 h−1)=s/dimensionless=s\tau_{knee}=h_0/(4\ln2\,h_{-1})=\text{s}/\text{dimensionless}=\text{s}τknee​=h0​/(4ln2h−1​)=s/dimensionless=s ✓.

import numpy as np
g, Si, qmax, f0, fc = 0.5, 1e-24, 1e-12, 5e9, 3.2e3
h_phi = g**2*Si/(qmax**2*4*np.pi**2)          # S_phi white-FM coefficient (rad^2·Hz)
h_m1  = h_phi*fc/f0**2                        # S_y = h_m1/f (dimensionless)
floor = np.sqrt(2*np.log(2)*h_m1)
print(f"{h_phi:.2e} {h_m1:.2e} {floor:.2e}")  # -> 6.33e-03 8.11e-19 1.06e-09
h0 = h_phi/f0**2
print(f"{h0:.2e} {1/(4*np.log(2)*fc)*1e6:.0f}")  # -> 2.53e-22 113

Simulation verification: the absolute floor level (lab_19 extension)​

lab_19 (simulations/lab_19_allan.py) has been extended to verify absolute values, not just slopes, doing three things:

  1. The integral family: scipy.integrate.quad computes I2,I3,I4I_2,I_3,I_4I2​,I3​,I4​ directly (up to 200π200\pi200π plus the analytic ⟨sin⁡4⟩=3/8\langle\sin^4\rangle=3/8⟨sin4⟩=3/8 tail), printing 0.7854, 0.6931, 1.0472, matching π/4\pi/4π/4, ln⁡2\ln2ln2, π/3\pi/3π/3 ✓.
  2. The floor of pure flicker FM: FFT shaping synthesizes y(t)y(t)y(t) with an exactly known absolute PSD — unit-variance white noise has one-sided PSD 2/fs2/f_s2/fs​, so shape with ∣H∣2=Starget/(2/fs)\lvert H\rvert^2=S_{target}/(2/f_s)∣H∣2=Starget​/(2/fs​) (function synth_y_from_psd; unlike power_law_y, which normalizes only the slope) — with h−1=8.11×10−19h_{-1}=8.11\times10^{-19}h−1​=8.11×10−19, 8 seeds, overlapping ADEV over τ=10…2000\tau=10\dots2000τ=10…2000 s, yielding measured/theory =1.004=1.004=1.004 (theory 2ln⁡2 h−1=1.06×10−9\sqrt{2\ln2\,h_{-1}}=1.06\times10^{-9}2ln2h−1​​=1.06×10−9).
  3. The full white＋flicker curve: superposing Sy=h0+h−1/fS_y=h_0+h_{-1}/fSy​=h0​+h−1​/f (both canonical coefficients), fs=1f_s=1fs​=1 MHz, 2222^{22}222 points, 6 seeds; the entire curve (knee included) deviates from h0/2τ+2ln⁡2 h−1\sqrt{h_0/2\tau+2\ln2\,h_{-1}}h0​/2τ+2ln2h−1​​ by at most 2.3%.

How to read it: the simulated points (blue) descend along the white-FM asymptote h0/2τ\sqrt{h_0/2\tau}h0​/2τ​ with slope −1/2-1/2−1/2 at small τ\tauτ, turn at τknee=113 μ\tau_{knee}=113\ \muτknee​=113 μs, then sit on the 1.06×10−91.06\times10^{-9}1.06×10−9 floor — the level agrees with theory to 0.4% (floor band). Two honest caveats: (a) the lowest frequency of the synthesized noise is truncated by the record length at fs/Nf_s/Nfs​/N, so at the largest τ\tauτ some flicker power is missing and the curve deviates slightly (included in the 2.3%); (b) this is a toy synthesis validating the "integral mathematics" — the floor level of a real oscillator is set by its real fcf_cfc​ and h−2ϕh^{\phi}_{-2}h−2ϕ​.

    • [E1] D. W. Allan, "Statistics of Atomic Frequency Standards," Proc. IEEE, vol. 54, no. 2, pp. 221–230, Feb. 1966. (the original ADEV proposal)

Riley, "Handbook of Frequency Stability Analysis," 2008) — the standard references for the power-law slope table and the overlapping-ADEV estimator.
    • The above are IEEE Std 1139-2008 (prior edition 1139-1999) and NIST SP 1065 (W. J. Riley, Handbook of Frequency Stability Analysis, 2008); volume/issue and edition details have been verified.

The corner fc=3.2f_c=3.2fc​=3.2 kHz of Example 3 comes from [P1] Eq.(24) (Example F of flicker_noise_upconversion).

Key takeaways​

  • ADEV σy(τ)\sigma_y(\tau)σy​(τ) is the time-domain counterpart of phase noise: from the same Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f), first convert Sy=(f2/f02)SϕS_y=(f^2/f_0^2)S_\phiSy​=(f2/f02​)Sϕ​, then substitute into σy2(τ)=2∫0∞Sy sin⁡4(πfτ)/(πfτ)2 df\sigma_y^2(\tau)=2\int_0^\infty S_y\,\sin^4(\pi f\tau)/(\pi f\tau)^2\,dfσy2​(τ)=2∫0∞​Sy​sin4(πfτ)/(πfτ)2df.
  • The essence of the definition σy2(τ)=⟨12(yˉk+1−yˉk)2⟩\sigma_y^2(\tau)=\langle\tfrac12(\bar y_{k+1}-\bar y_k)^2\rangleσy2​(τ)=⟨21​(yˉ​k+1​−yˉ​k​)2⟩ is the adjacent difference (a first difference, i.e. a high-pass) blocking slow drift and the unknown grand mean.
  • Five power-law slopes: white/flicker PM τ−1\tau^{-1}τ−1, white FM τ−1/2\tau^{-1/2}τ−1/2, flicker FM τ0\tau^{0}τ0 (floor), RW FM τ+1/2\tau^{+1/2}τ+1/2; the ADEV plot is a bathtub — drop, bottom out, climb — with the most stable point τopt\tau_{\text{opt}}τopt​ at the bottom.
  • Signature link: 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase noise ↔ white FM ↔ ADEV slope −1/2-1/2−1/2.
  • Why ADEV: the ordinary frequency variance does not converge for flicker/RW (it diverges with measurement duration); ADEV's differencing kernel goes like f2f^2f2 as f→0f\to0f→0, taming the low-frequency divergence and yielding a repeatable stability metric.
  • Example 2 shows how L(1MHz)=−100\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})=-100L(1MHz)=−100 dBc/Hz (5 GHz) yields a white SyS_ySy​ and σy(1ms)≈6.3×10−8\sigma_y(1\text{ms})\approx6.3\times10^{-8}σy​(1ms)≈6.3×10−8.
  • Prefactors, not just slopes: the substitution u=πfτu=\pi f\tauu=πfτ gives σy2=2hα(πτ)−(α+1)I2−α\sigma_y^2=2h_\alpha(\pi\tau)^{-(\alpha+1)}I_{2-\alpha}σy2​=2hα​(πτ)−(α+1)I2−α​; I2=π/4I_2=\pi/4I2​=π/4, I3=ln⁡2I_3=\ln2I3​=ln2, I4=π/3I_4=\pi/3I4​=π/3 ⇒ white FM h0/2τh_0/2\tauh0​/2τ, flicker floor 2ln⁡2 h−12\ln2\,h_{-1}2ln2h−1​ (τ\tauτ-independent), RW FM 2π23h−2τ\tfrac{2\pi^2}{3}h_{-2}\tau32π2​h−2​τ; the two PM rows must carry fhf_hfh​ because I1,I0I_1,I_0I1​,I0​ diverge at high frequency.
  • Where the ln⁡2\ln2ln2 comes from: power-reduce sin⁡4\sin^4sin4 into the 2u,4u2u,4u2u,4u harmonics, integrate by parts twice, then the Frullani-type ∫(cos⁡2u−cos⁡4u)/u du=ln⁡(4/2)\int(\cos2u-\cos4u)/u\,du=\ln(4/2)∫(cos2u−cos4u)/udu=ln(4/2); quad verifies 0.6931 ✓.
  • Canonical numbers (Example 3): fc=3.2f_c=3.2fc​=3.2 kHz ⇒ h−1=8.11×10−19h_{-1}=8.11\times10^{-19}h−1​=8.11×10−19, floor =1.06×10−9=1.06\times10^{-9}=1.06×10−9 (≈5.3\approx5.3≈5.3 Hz @ 5 GHz), τknee=1/(4ln⁡2fc)=113 μ\tau_{knee}=1/(4\ln2 f_c)=113\ \muτknee​=1/(4ln2fc​)=113 μs (≈0.36/fc\approx0.36/f_c≈0.36/fc​); floor ∝c0\propto c_0∝c0​ — symmetrization directly lowers the long-term stability floor. lab_19 measures measured/theory =1.004=1.004=1.004 on synthesized noise with exactly known absolute PSD.
